titleStmt.title: Using SMT to Hide Context Switch Times of Large Real-Time Tasksets

analytic.title: Using SMT to Hide Context Switch Times of Large Real-Time Tasksets

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Theoretical real-time research generally neglects context switch times. But in recent embedded applications which consist of dozens of threads with very short execution times, their impact is too serious to be ignored. We present a hard real-time scheduling algorithm that perfectly hides the context switch times of an arbitrary number of threads. It requires a Simultaneous Multithreaded (SMT) processor with at least two hardware thread slots and achieves a utilisation of 100%. The schedulability test is the same as for Earliest Deadline First (EDF) with a context switch time of zero.

The hard real-time threads are executed alternately in the two slots of the processor. The inactive slot is used to unload the preceding thread context to memory and to load the subsequent thread context from memory. By hardware the active slot is completely isolated, in order to avoid any influence of the context switch on the execution of the active thread. This isolation is extensive, hence if further SMT thread slots are available, they can be used to execute threads with lower real-time demands. Even the context switch hardware can be re-used for them, enabling a very high throughput of mixed real-time tasksets.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Simple single-threaded in-order processors are currently still the main platforms for embedded hard real-time systems, because this class of processors provides a tight Worst Case Execution Time (WCET) analysis that is essential for hard real-time systems. Modern features like out-of-order execution, dynamic branch prediction or multi-level caches extremely complicate the analysis, lead to overestimation and thus are avoided.

There are several proposals for novel hard real-time capable architectures [1], [2], [3], but they cannot solve the major problem of multithreaded hard real-time hardware: resources cannot be dynamically shared, because in the worst case all threads demand the same resource at the same time. There are only two solutions according to Barre et al. [4]: duplicate or time-slice the resources. Duplication leads to multi-core architectures, where everything is duplicated except the memory. In this paper we do not discuss multi-core solutions, instead we want to increase the single core performance. In future these cores might be assembled to a multi-core. Consequently we use time-slicing to distribute the execution time to the hard real-time threads, providing a much more flexible time distribution than the above mentioned alternative proposals.

When switching the execution from one thread to another, the complete register set of the thread (the thread context) must be saved and replaced by the register values of the new thread. Depending on the size of the register file, this can take a remarkable amount of time. These context switch times pose a serious problem in actual real-time systems, but mathematical scheduling theory mainly examines it inadequately.

One way to deal with context switches is to avoid them by prohibiting any thread interruptions (nonpreemptive scheduling). With this precondition, there are exactly two context switches per thread: one at the beginning of the execution and one at the end. Adding this constant context switch time to the execution time of the thread is a reliable method to comprise context switch times, but nonpreemptive schedules are not optimal and waste computing time.

In contrast preemptive scheduling allows arbitrary interruptions and can provide optimal utilisation of the processor. But it assumes a context switch time of zero, which is hard to implement. A possible solution is a multithreaded processor, which switches between multiple threads of execution without any time loss. This is achieved by duplicating the register set, in order to provide a separate register set per thread. However the hardware demand increases with every additional register set and therefore only a small number of parallel register sets (typically two to eight) is technically reasonable.

If there are more threads than supplied by the hardware, context switches to memory are inevitable, usually leading to multi-cycle context switching overhead. In this paper we present a solution to completely hide the context switch overhead of an arbitrary number of hard real-time threads, requiring only two thread slots of a Simultaneous Multithreaded (SMT) processor.

The highest priority thread is executed in complete isolation, as if it were the only thread on a single-threaded in-order processor, hence a standard WCET analysis can be applied. If multiple hard real-time threads are desired, each one is executed consistently for a time slice that corresponds to the rate of its deadline and period. The hardware scheduler uses the second thread slot to unload the previous and load the next thread context. At the time of the context switch the thread slots are swapped and the next thread continues execution without any context switch delay.

The real execution time of a hard real-time thread is often shorter than the WCET, the remaining time as well as fine grained latencies from branch and memory delays can be used to execute threads with lower real-time demands. Hence we provide a soft real-time scheduling algorithm that controls the number of Instructions Per Cycle (IPC) and a fair round robin policy for non-real-time threads.
The contributions of this paper are:

• A hard real-time scheduling algorithm that has the same schedulability and utilisation as Earliest Deadline First, but context switch times are hidden and therefore an arbitrary number of threads is allowed. • Non-hard real-time scheduling algorithms that use idle processor resources to improve overall throughput. • A detailed description of the convenient software interface and the hardware extensions that can be added to any in-order SMT processor.

The paper is organised as follows: the next section presents related work, while section III outlines the scheduling algorithms and the context switch mechanism. In section IV the hardware architecture is described and section V contains the evaluation. Finally section VI states our conclusions.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: This work intersects three fields of research: hard real-time capable architectures, SMT processors and hardware to speed up context switches. Furthermore previous work of our group is presented.

div.head: A. Multithreaded Hard Real-time Architectures
div.p: The Precision Timed (PRET) Architecture [1] uses static thread interleaving to execute exactly six predictable threads in parallel. As each thread is only executed every sixth cycle, no bypass network is needed, but the thread number is fixed. However the Real-time Virtual Multiprocessor (RVMP) [2] does not limit the number of threads by hardware and issues multiple instructions from multiple threads to multiple pipelines, but the pipelines must be identical and the mapping of threads to pipelines is static and repeated periodically. Both architectures have in common that they are able to execute multiple hard real-time threads, but the distribution of the execution time is very restricted and latencies cannot be used dynamically by other threads with lower real-time demands.

A completely different approach is implemented by the Virtual Simple Architecture (VISA) [3]: it guarantees the execution time of a simple hypothetical processor (comparable to a superscalar in-order processor), but executes the threads on a high-performance, speculative SMT processor. The progress of the speculative execution is monitored and compared to the guaranteed performance. If it is lower, the processor falls back to a direct, cycle-accurate emulation of the simple architecture to meet the deadlines. VISA is beneficial if the deadline is of wide scope, as it can be used to further increase the scope. But if there is only a small scope, there is not enough time to try the high-performance execution, because it must switch to the simple mode as soon as the remaining scope meets the WCET of the simple architecture. By contrast, our approach improves the real-time performance even with tight timing bounds.

div.head: B. Soft Real-time SMT Architectures
div.p: The first work on soft real-time scheduling for SMT processors [5] only profile threads to calculate an ideal co-schedule. Dorai and Yeung [6] try to preserve, as much as possible, the single-thread performance of a foreground thread, while allowing some progress to the background threads, but realtime guarantees are not considered.

It is common practice to control the number of Instructions Per Cycle (IPC) of soft real-time threads [7], [8], [9]. Cazorla et al. [7] determine the average IPC during a sample phase and afterwards in the tune phase the scheduler tries to reach a percentage of this IPC (the target IPC) by dynamically varying the amount of resources given to the real-time thread. In combination with prioritised resources, even multiple independent threads can be controlled without a sample phase [8]. Another approach uses a PID controller to stabilise the IPC [9]. Either the remaining resources can be used to execute non-real-time threads, or the clock rate can be reduced to save energy.

These IPC control architectures have two drawbacks: (i) they cannot absolutely guarantee the target IPC, thus they only provide soft real-time and (ii) they indirectly control the IPC via resource allocation or frequency scaling, whereas our scheduler directly controls the executed instructions and therefore exactly reaches the target IPC.

In contrast to all mentioned SMT architectures, our architecture fulfils the requirements, Barre et. al. [4] propose for an predictable SMT architecture where a static WCET analysis can be applied and therefore hard real-time scheduling is possible.

div.head: C. Hardware Context Switching
div.p: So far, all mentioned architectures provide only a fixed number of threads. With Dribbling Registers [10] the loading of a context from memory is done in the background, in advance of the actual context switch. At the time of the switch, the dribbling register set is exchanged with a real register set. This mechanism is comparable to our context switch of hard real-time threads, but the switch occupies free memory slots and therefore the duration of a context switch is hard to predict and not hard real-time capable.

The Balanced Multithreading [11] technique is similar to the context switching of our scheduler: Whenever there is a context switch, some special instructions are issued to the pipeline to unload the suspended thread to its virtual context in memory and to load the context of a new thread from memory. By contrast our scheduler uses a direct transfer between context memory and register set, to avoid thread interference within the pipeline.

In a Context Cache [12] only the registers that are involved in current calculations can be accessed quickly. If one is no longer used, it is written back to the actual context in memory. This approach is very flexible, but not real-time capable, as the state of the cache is not predictable due to thread interference.

div.head: D. Preliminary Own Work
div.p: The scheduler presented here is based on an in-order SMT processor. The characteristics of this class of SMT processors and how such a processor can be built by extending an arbitrary superscalar in-order processor is explained in [13].

In [14] the complete isolation of the highest priority thread, including a technique to delay lower priority memory accesses to avoid any influence on the highest priority thread execution is presented. The prospects of overlapping the execution time of soft real-time threads are studied in [15], but only for a small number of threads without context swapping to memory.

The three papers describe underlying technical details, whereas in this paper we present the hard real-time scheduling algorithm, the context switch mechanism and the hardware implementation of the scheduler.

div.head: III. MEMORY SNOOPING SCHEDULER
div.p: Each context of a thread is stored in a Thread Control Block (TCB) that is located in a special memory area called TCB memory. Our scheduler, the Memory Snooping Scheduler (MSS) decides which context should be swapped to the small number of hardware thread slots. Only one thread context at a time can be loaded from TCB memory to a slot or unloaded from a slot to TCB memory. A context switch consists of an unload and a subsequent load operation to the same slot. Both operations take a fixed number of cycles and the execution of the other thread slots continues, they are not affected in any case. The MSS acts independent of the pipeline, it is only controlled by the values in the TCBs.

The scheduler divides the execution time into small rounds of fixed length. Fig. 1 shows the distribution of threads to slots during one round, according to their real-time class: two slots are always reserved for the execution of hard real-time threads, but only one of them is active at a certain point of time. The other slots are filled with soft real-time threads at the beginning of a round. Later during a round, when the soft real-time threads reached the expected Instructions Per Cycle (IPC) rate, they are replaced by non-real-time threads.

div.head: A. Hard Real-time
div.p: The highest priority thread is executed in complete isolation, accordingly it is executed like a thread in a single-threaded architecture and the well-known techniques for single-threaded WCET analysis can be applied. If more than one hard real-time thread should be executed, the execution time of the highest priority thread must be distributed to them in the same way as a hard real-time taskset is scheduled to a single-threaded processor.

Such a taskset is typically described by the periodic task model [16], where threads are released periodically and have to complete before the next instance begins. Each thread τ i is characterised by the time between the release of two consecutive instances of the same thread (period T i ) and its WCET C i .

The basic idea of our scheduling algorithm was inspired by the Minimal Time Slicing algorithm of Serlin [16] and therefore called Dominant Time Slicing (DTS): the total execution time is split into small scheduling intervals, called rounds, with a fixed length of R cycles. During each round every thread is exclusively executed once. The duration of a thread's execution within an interval depends on its desired rate times the round length R and is called its Cycle Quantum
Schedulability is given, if the sum of the quanta is not greater than the round length:
div.formula: i Q i = R • i C i T i ≤ R(1)
div.p: Divided by R this is the optimal schedulability test, the same as for Earliest Deadline First (EDF).

For the optimal case, R must be the greatest common divider (GCD) of the periods and all quanta must be integer. If these conditions do not apply, or the minimum quantum is too small (see below), the quanta and the periods must be slightly adjusted: the quanta can be rounded up and the periods can be slightly prolonged to increase the GCD. But the effect of these adjustments is very small considering the scale: if the periods are given at an accuracy of 0.1 ms, the GCD is at least 0.1 ms which (at a clock rate of 100 MHz) equates a minimum round length of 10000 clock cycles. Then 50 threads lead to a maximum rounding overhead of 50 cycles per round or 0.5%.

Because the sequence of threads is fixed and there is only one counter that must be monitored, the hardware implementation of DTS is a lot simpler than that of deadline driven algorithms like EDF. But there is another difference, that is far more important: although the DTS algorithm activates more context switches, there is lower bound for the time between consecutive context switches: the minimum quantum.

The higher frequency of context switches does not matter, as they are hidden, but the hiding is only possible due to the known minimum time between context switches. Context switches indeed operate in the background, but their execution takes some time. If the inter context switch time is very short, i. e. the next context switch occurs although the previous has not been completed yet, the execution of the second context switch is delayed, and so the execution of all later threads.

But if the minimum time between two context switches is longer than the duration of a context switch (which is fixed by architecture), it is guaranteed that there is no interference and no subsequent delay. Even if this interval is shorter than the context switch time, the length of the round and all quanta can be multiplied with a constant factor in order to get a smallest quantum that is greater than the context switch time. At any point of time there is only one DTS thread active, therefore two slots are enough to schedule an arbitrary number of contexts, one for execution and one to load or unload to TCB memory. Fig. 2 illustrates the algorithm:

At the beginning of the first round, slot σ 1 executes thread τ 1 . While it is executed with highest priority, the context of thread τ 2 is loaded to slot σ 2 . As soon as τ 1 reaches its quantum (i. e. it was executed for Q 1 cycles), slot σ 2 gets the highest priority and slot σ 1 is disabled. Immediately after the switch, the context of τ 1 is unloaded to TCB memory and afterwards the context of thread τ 3 is loaded to slot σ 1 . Because of a proper selection of R, the time spent for these two tasks is less than Q 2 , the cycle quantum of thread τ 2 . From this time on slot σ 1 is frozen, it starts execution when the quantum border is reached and slot σ 2 is stopped.

The procedure continues till the end of the round, when everything starts again with the first thread context. The loading of τ 1 actually begins during the execution of the last thread, in order to guarantee a slot with ready thread τ 1 at the first cycle of the next round. If the quanta do not sum up to the round length (i.e. the processor is not fully utilised), there are slack cycles at the end of each round, when neither slot σ 1 nor slot σ 2 are active.

div.head: B. Soft Real-time
div.p: As no thread can occupy every functional unit in every cycle, there are always cycles where instructions from other than the hard real-time threads can be issued. Branch and memory delays are usable as well as the slack time, the gap between the actual completion of a hard real-time thread and its deadline. The remaining time can be used to execute soft real-time threads, which do not fail if a deadline is missed, but expect that it is met in the normal case. A common way to manage soft real-time threads is to control the number of executed Instructions Per Cycle (IPC) [9], [7], [8].

The Periodic Instruction Quantum (PIQ) algorithm divides the time into rounds in the same way as the DTS algorithm does, but execution of a thread is not disabled after a number of cycles, but after a certain number of executed instructions. This number is called Instruction Quantum q i and is the product of desired IPC and the round length R.

At the beginning of a round all thread slots, except the two reserved for DTS threads are filled with PIQ threads one after the other (if the slots are occupied by other threads, they must be unloaded first). As soon as the loading of a context to a thread slot has finished, the slot gets a priority and is enabled for execution. When a slot reaches its instruction quantum the slot is disabled, its context is unloaded to the TCB memory and the context of the next thread is loaded to the just unloaded slot. When these two transfers have been finished, the slot is re-enabled.

The assigned priorities are strictly descending, later loaded threads get lower priorities. As the first threads have higher priorities, they are executed more frequently and when one of them reaches its quantum, all threads with lower priorities are automatically lifted one priority level and thus execute faster (Fig. 3).

If all PIQ threads were executed once, the slots can be used for non-real-time threads (next section) or stay disabled until the beginning of the next round. The opposite, when threads have not completed their quantum at the end of a round (contrary to hard real-time threads, this is allowed for soft real-time threads) is worse: the scheduler unloads the uncompleted threads anyway and starts loading the same early PIQ threads as if all were satisfied. Later within the round the previously uncompleted threads are loaded again with the original quantum. Thus earlier threads are preferred, but overloading the system is avoided.

div.head: C. Non-real-time
div.p: As mentioned before, usually there is a slack of unused cycles at the end of each round, but its size oscillates heavily. Therefore it cannot be used for real-time threads, but additional threads without real-time constraints can use the remaining processing power. Such non-real-time threads may collect statistical data, supervise the correct functionality of components, etc. We propose the Round Robin Slack (RRS) algorithm that provides a fair distribution of the available execution time between the non-real-time threads. To reduce hardware costs, the instruction counters of the PIQ scheduler are reused.

At the beginning of a round all slots are occupied by hard and soft real-time threads. Not before all soft real-time threads were swapped to a slot and the first of these slots completed its quantum, a context switch to the first non-real-time thread can take place. As soon as another thread completes, the next non-real-time thread is loaded to the thread slot. Each of the RRS threads has a quantum and when it has been executed for the according number of instructions it is replaced by the next RRS thread. If all threads were activated once, the scheduler continues with the first RRS thread again.

The round robin replacement of the non-real-time threads is interrupted at the end of a round. Starting with the first cycle of the new round, one of the RRS threads is unloaded to TCB memory and replaced by the first PIQ thread. Directly after this context switch the next context switch takes place and replaces another RRS thread by a PIQ thread. The procedure continues until all thread slots (except the two reserved for DTS scheduling) are filled with PIQ threads.

The remaining quanta of the aborted threads are stored in the TCB when their contexts are written to TCB memory. The next time the thread context is loaded to a slot, this remaining quantum is added to its actual instruction quantum, to balance the execution times.

div.head: D. Interrupt Handling
div.p: Bandwidth preserving algorithms like the Sporadic Server [17] are usually used to deal with aperiodic interrupts. It provides a high priority server thread that preserves a fraction of the execution time for the execution of interrupts. Our MSS inherently provides this functionality: if the sum of DTS cycle quanta is less than the length of the round the remaining time is reserved for PIQ threads. Interrupt service threads should be inserted at the head of the PIQ list with the suspended flag set. On an interrupt signal, the flag of the related thread is cleared and the service routine will be executed after the DTS threads received their quanta in the current round.

div.head: IV. HARDWARE ARCHITECTURE
div.p: The scheduling is divided into three layers: The first layer is the issue stage of a prioritised in-order multithreaded processor. Its priorities are controlled by dedicated hardware (the second layer) that interprets the data from the software interface (third layer) and converts it to priorities and context switch commands. Fig. 4 shows the principal layout of a system that implements our MSS.

div.head: A. Base Processor Requirements (1st Layer)
div.p: The scheduler was designed to be as independent as possible from the underlying processor architecture. Therefore in this section we define the minimum requirements of the base processor pipeline and its interface to the second layer scheduler hardware. The CarCore processor [13] provides these requirements and we use it for the evaluation.

The base processor can be an SMT processor that issues one or more instructions from each thread simultaneously to multiple pipeline back-ends. There is no limitation on which pipeline back-end supports which subset of the instruction set, the subsets can even overlap or be identical. Even scalar multithreaded processors with only one pipeline back-end are supported. The only important requirements are the inorder execution for a predictable pipeline behaviour and the multithreading capability.

The pipeline stage that is responsible for dispatching instructions to the multiple functional units -the issue stage -is controlled by the second layer hardware via the signal PRIORITY. This signal provides a distinct priority for every slot and can differ from cycle to cycle. In every cycle, the issue stage tries to fill the functional units with instructions from the slot with the highest priority. If the highest priority slot cannot provide an appropriate instruction, an instruction from the second priority slot is taken, then from the third, and so on. The result of this assignment (which functional unit executes an instruction from which slot) is notified in every clock cycle via the ISSUED signal to the second layer (Fig. 4).

The preference of the highest priority slot should ensure that it is executed as if it were the only thread. If there are other parts of the pipeline (e.g. a memory interface with long latencies) that violate the total isolation of the highest priority slot, there are two possibilities: Either implement appropriate hardware to guarantee isolation [14], or consider delays by concurrent threads in the WCET analysis.

A slot is resumed by assigning a valid priority to it and suspended by a special invalid priority. If the priority is set invalid while a multi-cycle instruction is executed, the execution must be completed first, before the slot can be disabled and a context switch can take place. Hence there is a third wire between the issue stage and the second layer: The ALIVE signal notifies that a thread is still active in a slot. ALIVE is set, as soon as a slot gets a valid priority and cleared as soon as the priority is invalid and the current instruction has completed. Fig. 5 shows the state transition diagram of the issue stage.

div.head: B. Hardware Outside the Pipeline (2nd Layer)
div.p: The second layer is the heart of the scheduler: here the bookkeeping of the execution counters takes place and the execution of the threads in the pipeline (first layer) is controlled according to the specifications of the third layer. Furthermore it suspends or resumes thread slots, specifies the priorities of the slots and switches contexts between slots and memory. The functional parts are:

1) Context Switch Unit (CSU): Provides a direct link between the register files and the TCB memory. On behalf of the Priority Control Unit (PCU), the whole register set of a slot is written to a specific TCB or vice versa. When loading 2) Memory Snooping Unit (MSU): Monitors write accesses from the pipeline to the TCB memory and filters those accesses that modify scheduling parameters of currently active TCBs. The new values are buffered and provided to the PCU. Accesses to TCBs, that are not executed in a thread slot at the moment, are ignored, because the PCU does not use them. Therefore the only way for scheduling parameters of a nonresident TCB to arrive at the MSU is via the CSU when the TCB is loaded to a thread slot. The MSU also monitors stores to TCB 0, where the global scheduling data is located.

3) Quantum Watchdog (QWD): There is a counter for every thread slot and depending on the individual scheduling algorithm, the counter is either decreased at every clock cycle (DTS) or whenever an instruction of the specific thread is issued (PIQ/RRS). When a counter becomes zero, the PCU is notified to launch appropriate response. Likewise the end of a round is notified.

div.head: 4) Priority Control Unit (PCU):
div.p: The central unit of the scheduler. As soon as the QWD gives notice of the end of a quantum, the execution of the respective thread slot is stopped by setting its priority to be invalid. If a DTS thread is stopped, the priority of the other DTS thread slot is raised to the maximum to avoid any wasted cycles. After setting the priority to be invalid, the PCU has to wait until the ALIVE signal from the issue stage acknowledges the termination of the thread slot (It may take some cycles, if the thread is interrupted within a multi-cycle instruction that must be finished first). Afterwards the PCU directs the CSU to unload the register file to the appropriate TCB memory location.

Again, this takes some cycles and the PCU uses the time to decide, which thread should be loaded instead of the old one. If a DTS thread was stopped, it is replaced by the next DTS thread or -at the end of a round -by the first DTS thread for the next round. Else the next PIQ thread is loaded or if all soft real-time threads were executed once this round, the next RRS thread is chosen. When the unloading of the old thread is completed, the CSU begins to load the TCB that was picked by the PCU. Finally the PCU sets the slot priority to a valid number and waits for the next event the QWD announces.

The behaviour of the PCU is slightly different, if the beginning of a new round is announced. First, the slot with the first DTS thread gets the highest priority and the other DTS slot with the last DTS thread from the former round is suspended. Then the CSU unloads the last DTS thread and loads the context of the next DTS thread to the same slot. After that, the PCU searches a slot that executes a RRS thread, suspends it and directs the CSU to replace it by the first PIQ thread.

When writing the RRS register set to memory, the remaining instruction quantum of the RRS thread is written to the TCB, too. The value is written to the entry overhead, in order to add this number to the regular quantum, when the thread is executed for the next time. After this context switch, the priority of the slot is set to the appropriate value and the CSU begins with the next context switch from a RRS to a PIQ thread. The procedure continues until all RRS threads are replaced or there is no more PIQ thread to resume.

As the context switches take several cycles, it could happen, that the QWD reports the end of a quantum, while the CSU is still busy. In such a case, the PCU immediately sets the priority of the second completed thread to the lowest possible value and starts the context switch when the current switch has finished (from this time on the priority is set to invalid).

div.head: C. Software Interface (3rd Layer)
div.p: All scheduling parameters and thread contexts are located in a separate memory area, the so-called TCB memory. Regular read and write accesses by load and store instructions are allowed and necessary, as the latter ones are the only way to modify the scheduling parameters. But besides these, there must be a read and a write port to the CSU. The accesses by the CSU are used to swap the register files to the TCB memory and vice versa. Because the total duration must be limited by a fixed upper bound, they must not be delayed by load or store instructions.

There are no further accesses to this memory area, in particular the priority control unit does not write to it, no scheduling data is modified by the PCU and it does not read anything from the memory. This fact, and the simple structure of the scheduling data ensures that the data can be kept consistent without synchronisation between PCU and memory (an explanation follows at the end of this section). Nevertheless, the PCU has to know the scheduling parameters. Therefore it keeps track of the write accesses to the TCB memory, filters it and logs the relevant information. This technique gives the scheduler its name: Memory Snooping Scheduler (MSS). Memory snooping is possible because of the special structure of the TCB memory. The TCB memory is organised as an array of TCBs with a fixed length l. The TCBs contain the complete context (all regular and special registers, including the program counter) and four scheduling parameters (see Tab. I).

Every entry in the array can hold a thread context, except the first one (TCB 0), which contains the global scheduling data: the length of a round and 3 pointers, each pointing to a singly linked list that contains the TCBs of the corresponding scheduling class (DTS, PIQ, RRS). The entry next in each TCB is the link between the TCBs.

If singly linked lists are modified in the right way, they are consistent at any point of time, without the need of special atomic instructions: when inserting Y between X and Z, first Y.next is set to Z, then X.next to Y. Therefore no special instruction to synchronise between memory and scheduling hardware is needed. Although the memory writes are not restricted, the scheduler can go through the list at any time and will never get into an undefined TCB. Nevertheless there must be some synchronisation between threads if more than one thread can modify the scheduling lists, the consistency is only given between hardware and memory, not between threads.

div.head: V. EVALUATION
div.p: We used 13 benchmarks from the EEMBC automotive benchmark suite [18] and 6 benchmarks from the Mälardalen WCET group [19], Tab. II shows their average IPCs. Compiled with the HighTec GNU C/C++ compiler for TriCore [20] and executed on the CarCore Processor [13] the total average IPC of all threads is 0.480.

div.head: A. Hardware Base
div.p: CarCore is a 32-bit dual-issue in-order SMT processor with Infineon Tricore [21] instruction set. Two models with identical timing are available, a SystemC model, where parameters can easily be altered and a VHDL model for FPGA synthesis on the Altera Stratix II EP2S180F1020C3 device. Tab. III compares the total size of the processor to the size of our MSS extension, depending on the number of hardware thread slots. The instruction memory is on-chip memory with zero latency and the data memory external SD-RAM with 3 cycles latency. The loading of a context takes 21 cycles, while the unloading takes 19 cycles.

div.head: B. Reasonable Number of Thread Slots
div.p: To determine the reasonable number of hardware thread slots that still provide nearly maximum throughput, context switches are not considered, instead there is exactly one thread per slot and the slots are scheduled by fixed priorities (the slot with the lowest number has the highest priority) to get the maximum average IPC. To cover a reliable number of cases, each combination of two benchmarks is executed for five times, every time with a different combination of benchmarks in the remaining thread slots. All in all, for each slot number, 19 × 19 × 5 = 1805 tasksets were executed for 1 million cycles each. We measure the throughput of the processor by the number of executed instructions per cycle (IPC). The maximum of the IPC is two, because the CarCore processor can issue two instructions per cycle to its two pipeline backends.

As Tab. IV illustrates, the average IPCs of the thread slots declines exponentially with lower priority, the thread slot with the eighth priority is almost never executed, therefore 7 is the absolute maximum for a reasonable number of slots. Even the benefit of a sixth and seventh slot is questionable comparing the throughput increase to the hardware demand. Furthermore Tab. IV shows that the IPC of the highest priority thread declines when the number of slots is increased. That is because the highest priority thread is not completely isolated, but interferes with concurrent threads when accessing memory.

The interference can be avoided by delaying lower priority memory accesses, whenever they would collide with the highest priority thread (see [14] for details). But thereby the overall throughput is seriously decreased, as Tab. V shows. In return the performance of the highest priority thread is the same as if it were executed single-threaded, because the lower priority threads do not delay it.

div.head: C. Size of the Quantum
div.p: The utilisation of the processor is decreased by context switches, because the affected thread slot is suspended during a context switch. Therefore a higher context switch frequency should imply a lower total IPC. To analyse this relation, Fig. 6. Overall IPC depending on quantum and number of thread slots tasksets of 8 threads are scheduled by RRS with varied quantum. Fig. 6 shows the average total IPC of 100 randomly chosen tasksets, depending on the quantum and the number of thread slots.

Only for small slot numbers (2 and 3, barely for 4) the size of the quantum has an effect on the total IPC, for slot numbers higher than 4 there is none. To explain this behaviour, it must be examined what happens when a context switch takes place: The issue stage has one slot less to chose from and behaves as if the architecture offers one slot less. The effect of a missing slot on the utilisation is quite dynamic: as Tab. IV and Tab. V show, the IPC difference between successive slot numbers shrinks with growing slot number. From 5 slots on, the difference is so small, that an influence on the utilisation of swapped tasksets is nearly invisible. For a quantum of 500 cycles or more, the degradation by context switches nearly disappears.

div.head: D. Comparison With Software Scheduler
div.p: To compare the MSS with a software scheduler we calculate a very rough approximation of the power consumption. When implementing the DTS algorithm by software on a singlethreaded processor, there is a context switch for every thread in every round. With N threads and a context switch time of S cycles, the length of a round is prolonged to R = R+S •N . Consequently the clock rate f SW must be increased to meet the deadlines:
div.formula: f SW = f 0 R + S • N R(2)
div.p: The energy consumption is proportional to the third power of the frequency, consequently the energy consumption of the software scheduler is
div.formula: E SW = E 0 R + S • N R 3(3)
div.p: with the energy consumption E 0 of the single-threaded processor at frequency f 0 . Assuming that the energy consumption is proportional to the design size A, the energy consumption E HW of the hardware scheduler can be approximated by The hardware scheduler consumes less power than its software equivalent, if E HW < E SW . We measured a software context switch time of S = 359 for the CarCore. Together with the design size A HW = 21129 of the processor with two thread slots and A 0 = 14808 for the single-threaded design size (Tab. III), we get
div.formula: E HW = E 0 A HW A 0(4)
div.p: If the average quantum of the threads R N is less than 2850, the MSS consumes less power than a software scheduler on a single-threaded processor, e. g. the hardware scheduler is beneficial if the sum of the quanta of 20 threads is less than 57000 cycles.

Another possibility would be to implement DTS on a twothreaded processor with the secondary thread slot doing the context switching by software. In this case the frequency need not be scaled, but the architecture is not hard real-time capable any more, because the execution time of the context switch thread cannot be bounded, as it depends on the resources the primary thread does not use. Anyway we measured the maximum execution time of a thread that is executed in parallel to the benchmarks and does nothing except constantly switching its context. The context switch time depends heavily on the benchmark (500 to 1300 cycles on average, depending on the benchmark), the maximum we measured was 1607, Using free memory access slots of the highest priority thread instead of a separate port to TCB memory represents a tradeoff between a two-threaded software solution and the MSS. This approach is not hard real-time capable with state-ofthe-art analysis tools either; but an extended analysis of the hard real-time threads might enable the calculation of a safe minimum round length. Such an analysis must comprise the calculation of the minimum number of free memory access slots during one round. This analysis is not easy but basically possible. At least it is far simpler than the analysis of a background software scheduler. Our experiments show, that on average within 400 cycles there are 40 free memory slots that do not slow down the highest priority thread. The maximum interval for the examined benchmarks was 755 cycles.

div.head: E. Soft Real-Time Overlapping
div.p: To show the potential of overlapping the execution times of large real-time tasksets, we compared DTS and PIQ scheduling when executing large tasksets. Each taskset consists of 20 threads, each executing one randomly chosen benchmark. When DTS scheduled, each thread is executed for 500 cycles per round, resulting in a round length of 10000 cycles. For PIQ scheduling the cycle quantum of 500 is multiplied with the individual benchmark IPC (Tab. II) to get an instruction quantum. 400 randomly generated tasksets were examined on architectures with 2 to 8 slots and 20 slots (baseline with no context switches). Every combination of taskset and slot number was executed for 10000 rounds. The name of a taskset consists of 20 letters, one for each thread, see Tab. II for the thread abbreviations.

The DTS scheduled threads always use the complete round of 10000 cycles, the unused latency cycles are spread over the whole round. With PIQ scheduling the execution times of the threads are moved to the beginning of the round and at the end of each round there remains a slack of many cycles, when no PIQ thread is executed. The "useful" length of a roundthe number of cycles from the beginning of a round to the point of time when the context switch of the last PIQ thread to memory has completed -has a wide variation (Fig. 7,8,9). But 389 out of 400 tasksets (97%) reproduce a Gaussian distribution (Fig. 9), fortunately with sharp boundaries. Fig. 10 shows these boundaries and the average useful length depending on the number of hardware thread slots. The min, max and avr graphs show the minimum, maximum and average useful length of any round of any taskset with the given thread slot number. With increasing number of thread slots, all three lines converge to the value for a schedule without context switches to memory (horizontal lines). With 4 thread slots, every PIQ thread has reached its quantum on average after 50% of the round, not a single round of any taskset occupies more than 65% of a round. Hence one third of the processor performance can be used for additional threads.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: We presented a hardware extension to schedule an arbitrary number of hard real-time threads to an in-order SMT processor with only two hardware thread slots. The additional hardware pays off, if the average time between two context switches is less than 2850 cycles. Therefore it is appropriate to tasksets with a great number of threads and short individual execution times.

With small enhancements of the hard real-time scheduler it is possible to execute an arbitrary number of threads with lower real-time demands in additional thread slots. A soft realtime algorithm that directly controls the IPC and a fair round robin algorithm are available. Supplementing the two slots for hard real-time execution by three additional hardware slots for soft and non-real-time thread scheduling can double the overall throughput, if threads with adequate real-time characteristics are available.
